SLIDES:
My sister’s cleverer than me.

Short adjective → -er + than. than is weak here: it sounds like  th’n.

My brother isn’t as confident as my sister.

as … as = the same amount. With not, it means less.

I’m taller than my parents.

One syllable → -er. Never more tall.

My youngest brother isn’t as lazy as I am.

the youngest = one of three or more. as lazy as compares two.

Warm-up: Let a weak student answer with one word. Do not correct the character adjectives yet - they arrive in stage 2.
6 minutes. The counting-up moment is what makes the reading text land later.
Vocabulary: This is the syllabus set for the row. Drill the stress: SO-ciable, CRE-ative, hard-WOR-king.
confident/sociable and smart/creative are the pairs learners merge. Task 4 exists for exactly that.
Grammar: Spend your time on the two errors that survive to B2: double comparatives (more taller) and the missing as (as tall than).
6.3 is recognition only. Never turn it into a repetition drill.
Practice: Quantifiers from Lesson 14. Do not skip it - it is the only place quantity is forced this lesson.
Transformation and correct-the-mistake carry the weight here, not the multiple choice.
Reading: Ask the pre-reading question before they see the text. Ninety seconds for the gist task, then re-read for detail.
Secondary input. One short task only - do not build a second comprehension sequence on it.
Speaking: The second run is where the language sticks. Feedback after the swap, not during.
much / a bit + comparative. Most students will avoid it unless you ask.
Wrap: Say the word quantifiers out loud. Students should hear that Lesson 14 came back.

Stage 3 · Grammar

Comparing two, and comparing all

The meaning is easy. The form is where the marks are lost.

Read these four sentences from the text in stage 5.
  • A confident student got more attention than a shy one.
  • Introverts are just as creative as extroverts.
  • They are usually more patient, and they are often better listeners.
  • In many offices the loudest voice was also the most powerful voice.
Which sentence compares one thing with all the others?
The three forms
AdjectiveComparative — two thingsSuperlative — one above all
one syllable: quietquieter than her brotherthe quietest person here
ending -y: happyhappier than last yearthe happiest day of my life
two or more syllables: confidentmore confident than methe most confident student
irregular: good / bad / farbetter / worse / further thanthe best / the worst / the furthest
the same: as … asShe is as hard-working as her sister.  —  He isn’t as patient as you.
size of the differenceShe is much quieter than me.  /  He is a bit more confident than his sister.
Quantity recycledThere isn’t much noise in the library.  —  She hasn’t got many close friends.
The rules that matter
  • Two things → comparative + than. One thing above all others → the + superlative.
  • Short words take -er / -est. Longer words take more / the most. Use one or the other, never both: not more taller, not the most tallest.
  • as … as needs both words. as tall than me is the most common mistake at this level.
  • To say how big the difference is, put much or a bit in front: much cheaper, a bit more expensive.
  • You met quantifiers in Lesson 14. They come back in task 5 of the next stage.
Listen. Which sentence do you hear?

In fast speech than and as almost disappear. Listen for the ending of the adjective instead.

Full grammar reference — Comparatives and superlatives

Form

Short adjectivesold → older than → the oldest · big → bigger → the biggest
Ending in -yhappy → happier → the happiest
Long adjectivespatient → more patient than → the most patient
Irregulargood → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst
Equalas creative as · not as confident as
Making it strongermuch / far more patient · a bit / slightly quieter

Spelling and sound

Doubling: big → bigger, hot → hotter. -y → -ier: easy → easier. Two syllables ending in -er, -ow, -y usually take -er: quieter, narrower.

When and why we use it

  • Comparative for two things; superlative for three or more, or for the whole group.
  • Than follows a comparative; the comes before a superlative.
  • as … as says the two are equal; not as … as says the first one is less.
  • The superlative is often followed by in or ever: the best book in the shop, the best book I have ever read.

Signal words

than · the … est · the most · as … as · ever · much / a bit

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • She is more taller than me. → She is taller than me.Never both more and -er.
  • He is the most fast runner. → He is the fastest runner.Short adjective takes -est.
  • She is as patient than me. → She is as patient as me.as … as.
  • It is more good. → It is better.Irregular form.

Don’t confuse it with

Use the with a superlative but not with a comparative: the biggest city, but bigger than Almaty.

Stage 5 · Main input

The quiet ones

The main text of the lesson.

Before you read. Look at the title. Who do you think “the quiet ones” are?

The quiet ones

Some people love a big group. They talk to everyone, they share their ideas quickly, and they feel happy when the room is looking at them. We call these people extroverts. Other people are different. They think first and speak later, they prefer a small group or an empty room, and they often do their best work alone. These are introverts — the quiet ones.

For a long time, most schools and most companies wanted the first type. A confident, sociable student got more attention than a shy one. In many offices the loudest voice in the meeting was also the most powerful voice. But is that fair?

The writer Susan Cain says no. Her best-selling book Quiet argues that introverts are just as creative and just as hard-working as extroverts. They are usually more patient, too, and they are often better listeners. Their ideas are not louder. They are simply slower — and sometimes they are the strongest ideas in the room.

Cain says something more surprising as well: a team of only extroverts is not the best team. A good team needs both. The talkers move a project forward; the quiet ones notice the problem nobody mentioned.

Of course, nobody is one hundred per cent one type. Most of us are a bit of both, and we change with the situation. The important thing is not to become somebody else. If you are the quietest person in your class, that is not a weakness. It is a different kind of strength.

Sources. Written for this course. The argument it summarises — that introverts are undervalued in schools and offices, and that mixed teams work better — is from Susan Cain, Quiet (2012). No wording is taken from the book.
